lede: Gases cross into and out of blood at a surface built for the job: large, thin, moist and well supplied with blood. Lungs do it with millions of alveoli and a leaf does it with air spaces. Exercise changes how fast and how deeply you breathe.
can: List the six adaptations of a respiratory surface and what each gives.
Apply the same list to a leaf.
Use numbers from a breathing-rate graph to compare two people.

text: Respiratory surfaces, and what exercise does to your breathing

md: Every breath ends in millions of tiny air sacs wrapped in blood vessels. Oxygen crosses a wall one cell thick and carbon dioxide comes back the other way. Run upstairs and you breathe faster and deeper to keep that exchange going.

prompt: Why is the wall of an alveolus only one cell thick?
options: It gives a short diffusion distance
It gives a large surface area
answer: It gives a short diffusion distance
explain: Thin means a short distance to diffuse across, so gases move quickly. Surface area comes from the number of alveoli, not the thickness of one.

md:
Pair each adaptation with its reason and the marks look after themselves.
**Large surface area** (millions of alveoli) — more room for gases to cross at once.
**Thin** (one cell thick) — a short diffusion distance.
**Moist** — gases dissolve before they diffuse.
**Permeable** — gases can pass straight through the wall.
**Good blood supply** — blood carries the gases away.
**Diffusion gradient maintained** — because blood keeps removing oxygen and delivering carbon dioxide, the difference in concentration never disappears.

prompt: Why does being moist help an alveolus?
explain: Gases dissolve first, so a moist lining lets them cross.

title: Why the last two are not the same mark
md: 'Good blood supply' describes the **apparatus** — lots of capillaries. 'Maintains the diffusion gradient' describes the **consequence** — the concentration difference is kept up, so diffusion keeps going. CCEA lists both, so an answer that gives one is halfway. The blood is what stops the alveolus filling up with oxygen and stopping.

alt: Light micrograph of lung tissue at 200 times magnification: a mesh of thin pink-stained walls enclosing hundreds of empty air spaces of different sizes, with a large airway at the lower left and small blood vessels in the walls. Leader lines marked A, B, C and D and a list of four structure names are printed beside it as a labelling exercise.
caption: Real lung tissue at ×200. Every pale space is an air space, and every pink line between them is a wall about one cell thick.
prompt: Using this photograph, give two pieces of visible evidence that lung tissue is adapted for rapid gas exchange.
Which adaptation is the reason the concentration difference between the alveolus and the blood never disappears?
answer: good blood supply | blood supply | the blood supply
explain: The blood keeps carrying oxygen away and bringing carbon dioxide, so the diffusion gradient is maintained.

md: **Plants have respiratory surfaces too**, and the specification says so in as many words. A leaf is thin, its spongy mesophyll has a huge moist surface area, its walls are permeable, and photosynthesis using the carbon dioxide keeps a diffusion gradient going. Same six ideas, different organism — which is exactly how CCEA likes to set an unfamiliar-context question.

md: During exercise muscles respire faster, so they need more oxygen and make more carbon dioxide. Breathing changes in **two** ways: the **rate** goes up (more breaths each minute) and the **depth** goes up (more air in each breath). CCEA names both in the outcome, so an answer that gives only 'you breathe faster' is half an answer.

title: GCSE Biology Revision "Exercise"
why: Twelve minutes on what exercise does to breathing and heart rate, with the same depth-and-rate distinction CCEA marks. Watch it once, then answer the question underneath from memory.

prompt: Exercise changes breathing in two ways. Which pair is right?
options: the rate and the depth of breathing
the rate and the temperature of breathing
the depth and the direction of breathing
answer: the rate and the depth of breathing
explain: Rate is how many breaths a minute; depth is how much air in each one. The outcome names both, so both are marking points.

md: Read this graph in three parts. **Before** (0 to 10 minutes) both lines are flat: those are the **resting** breathing rates, 16 for X and 12 for Y. **During** (10 to 25 minutes, so 15 minutes of exercise) both rise and then level off. **After**, both fall — but Y is back to its resting rate by 40 minutes and X is not.

prompt: Use the graph. For how many minutes did the students exercise?
explain: Exercise runs from 10 minutes to 25 minutes, so 25 − 10 = 15 minutes. March 2026 examiners reported that fewer candidates worked this out than read the start time.

title: March 2026 B1 Foundation Q7
md: Candidates had to say which student was fitter and give evidence. Most gave two correct pieces, but **fewer noted that Y's resting breathing rate was lower**. Only the more able drew the recovery line **levelling out** at the right time rather than plunging to the axis. And the unit overview says it plainly: use evidence **from the graph** in your interpretation and conclusions.

prompt: Which piece of evidence shows that student Y is fitter?
explain: A lower resting rate — the one candidates most often miss.

md: **Three pieces of evidence that Y is fitter**, each a number off the graph: a lower **resting** rate (12 against 16 breaths per minute); a lower **highest** rate during exercise (28 against 36); and a **faster recovery** — Y is back to resting by 40 minutes while X is still at 18. Quote the numbers and the marks are safe.

prompt: Student X's breathing rate rose from 16 at rest to 36 breaths per minute. What is the percentage increase?
explain: 36 − 16 = 20; 20 ÷ 16 × 100 = 125%. Divide by the resting value, which is the one you started from.

md:
List the six adaptations of a **respiratory surface** and what each gives.
Explain why the wall is **thin** and why blood supply matters.
Apply the same list to a **leaf**.
Say that exercise changes **rate** and **depth**.
Use graph numbers to say which student is fitter.

A matching item worth four marks — one ruled line from each adaptation to its explanation, and some series print more explanations than adaptations. The exercise half is a graph question of six to nine marks where every mark wants a number from the graph. Stuck: read a value off and quote it in the answer.
